Gamma Count Distribution

Source: R/gcount.R
GammaCount.Rd

Density, distribution function, quantile function, and random generation for the gamma renewal count distribution (Winkelmann, 1995): the number of events in a time window when the times between events are independent gamma variables.

Usage

dgcount(x, shape, rate, time = 1, log = FALSE)

pgcount(q, shape, rate, time = 1, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

qgcount(p, shape, rate, time = 1, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

rgcount(n, shape, rate, time = 1)

Arguments

x

vector of (non-negative integer) quantiles.

shape

vector of (positive) shape parameters \(a\) of the gamma inter-arrival times. \(a = 1\) is the Poisson distribution, \(a > 1\) gives underdispersion and \(a < 1\) overdispersion.

rate

vector of (positive) rate parameters \(b\) of the gamma inter-arrival times.

time

vector of (positive) lengths \(t\) of the observation window. Default 1.

log, log.p

logical; if TRUE, probabilities p are given as log(p).

q

vector of quantiles.

lower.tail

logical; if TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(Y \leq y)\), otherwise \(P(Y > y)\).

p

vector of probabilities.

n

number of observations. If length(n) > 1, the length is taken to be the number required.

Value

dgcount gives the probability mass, pgcount the distribution function, qgcount the quantile function, and rgcount random deviates. The length of the result is determined by n for rgcount, and is the maximum of the lengths of the numerical arguments for the other functions.

Details

Let the times between events be independent Gamma(shape = \(a\), rate = \(b\)) variables and let \(N(t)\) be the number of events completed by time \(t\) (the process starts with an event at time 0). With \(G(s; c)\) the distribution function of a Gamma(\(c\), 1) variable at \(s = bt\) (pgamma(s, c)), $$P(N(t) \leq y) = 1 - G(bt; (y + 1)a), \qquad P(N(t) = y) = G(bt; ya) - G(bt; (y + 1)a),$$ with \(G(bt; 0) = 1\). Only the product \(bt\) enters the distribution. With \(a = 1\) the inter-arrival times are exponential and \(N(t)\) is Poisson with mean \(bt\).

The mean is \(E[N(t)] = \sum_{k \geq 1} G(bt; ka)\), which is approximately (but not exactly) \(bt / a\) for large \(bt\); the expected count is generally not proportional to the window length \(t\), so lengthening the window is not the same as a log-exposure offset.

Probabilities are differences of gamma distribution functions, taken between the pair of tail probabilities that is not close to one. When the shape \(a\) is very small the two terms are nearly equal and some relative accuracy (about \(\log_{10}(1/a)\) digits) is lost. Both tails of the distribution function are computed directly with pgamma(). rgcount() uses inversion of the distribution function.

References

Winkelmann, R. (1995). Duration dependence and dispersion in count-data models. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 13(4), 467-474.

Kharrat, T., Boshnakov, G. N., McHale, I. and Baker, R. (2019). Flexible regression models for count data based on renewal processes: the Countr package. Journal of Statistical Software, 90(13), 1-35.

Examples

dgcount(0:6, shape = 2, rate = 6)
#> [1] 0.01735127 0.13385262 0.29447576 0.29830012 0.17209622 0.06383205 0.01646347
# shape = 1 gives the Poisson distribution with mean rate * time
all.equal(dgcount(0:10, shape = 1, rate = 1.5, time = 2), dpois(0:10, 3))
#> [1] TRUE
pgcount(3, shape = 0.5, rate = 1.5)
#> [1] 0.5578254
qgcount(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), shape = 2, rate = 6)
#> [1] 1 3 4
set.seed(6)
y <- rgcount(2000, shape = 3, rate = 12)
c(mean = mean(y), var = var(y))   # underdispersed
#>     mean      var 
#> 3.676500 1.428562
